title: Shipping a Small Side Project End to End
summary: Notes from finally shipping a weekend project instead of letting it rot in a private repo — scope small, ship ugly, iterate later.
body:
I have a graveyard of half-built side projects, and honestly, most of them died from the same disease: scope creep before the first version ever shipped. This month I finally broke the pattern and shipped something small end to end, so I wanted to write down what actually worked.

## Rules I set for myself

1. **Pick a scope so small it feels almost embarrassing.** If it doesn't feel a little too simple, it's still too big.
2. **No new dependencies unless something breaks without one.** It's easy to lose a weekend to tooling instead of the actual idea.
3. **Deploy on day one**, even with a single hardcoded page. Getting a real URL out early keeps the project honest.

## What actually happened

The first deployable version took about two hours. It was ugly — no styling to speak of, a single page, hardcoded content. But it was *live*, and that changed how I thought about the next steps. Every feature after that got compared against "is this worth delaying the next deploy for," and most weren't.

> The version you ship beats the version you're still perfecting.

## What's next

I'm going to keep iterating in public rather than batching up a big rewrite. If you're sitting on a project that's 80% done and has been for months, my advice is simple: cut scope until you can ship *something* this week, then build from there.
author: Charlie Cunningham
